newsitem.title: USA: US envoys see Egypt-Israel gas pipeline on track.
newsitem.headline: US envoys see Egypt-Israel gas pipeline on track.

text.p: Negotiations for a proposed gas pipeline from Egypt to Israel has remained on track despite the outbreak of violence in the Middle East, according to U.S. ambassadors to the region.

The pipeline, dubbed the 'Peace Pipeline' by U.S. officials, is seen as a significant step in U.S. policy toward trying to ensure lasting peace in the Middle East through shared economic development in the region.

"Nothing has led this project to go off track, despite the violence" between Palestinians and Israelis, Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade, Stuart Eizenstat, told business associates at a New York symposium on Monday.
"We call this the 'Peace Pipeline,'" said Eizenstat. "It's important to delink political problems from economic integration."
He praised the project as the largest regional venture in in decades and said it would open up a huge opportunity for U.S. energy companies in the Middle East.
An executive with Amoco, which is part of team that proposed the pipeline, confirmed that talks between the Israeli and Eyptian government are continuing.
"Negotiations are still on going," said the executive, participating in the conference sponsored by the Business Council for International Understanding.
"The pipeline is a commercially viable project that is a function of volumes and values," he said, adding Egypt has huge proven gas reserves.
Amoco comprises 33 percent of the Egypt Trans Gas Company, which proposed the Egyptian-Israeli pipeline.
Agip SpA has a 33 percent holding and Egypt Gas has 34 percent in the company.

According to Amoco executives, gas for the pipeline project will be extracted from the Nile Delta Basin, which is emerging as a 'world class' natural gas basin. The pipeline is to run from Egypt's Port Said to the Israeli Port of Haifa, near the Gaza Strip, with links to Jericho and Jordan.

The pipeline is also seen as an indication of the emerging demand in the Middle East for natural gas, which is being used to power electricity plants to serve rural areas and fire the increasing number of petrochemical plants in the Gulf.

"There is so much gas in the region that there is not a power station being built now or in the future that is not gas driven," said Charles Kestenbaum, Senior Commercial Officer, American Embassy Abu Dhabi.
He added that several Gulf countries which have reached their oil production ceiling due to OPEC limitations are beginning to see gas liquids as a source of income.
"Condensates are not part of the oil quota," said Kestenbaum, adding he expects large opportunities for U.S. and other foreign investors in the region's energy sector.
